canonical_statement: The review aims to describe PI3K/Akt pathway roles across cancer phenotypes, summarize the status of PI3K/Akt inhibitors, and discuss combination strategies with conventional cancer therapies.
The authors propose that inhibitors targeting the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, either alone or combined with other therapies, represent an effective strategy for cancer treatment.
The review describes aberrant PI3K/Akt pathway activation in cancer through alterations involving PIK3CA, PTEN, Akt, TSC1, and mTOR.
PI3K converts PIP2 to PIP3, which recruits Akt, and activated Akt regulates downstream substrates including mTOR.
Class I PI3Ks comprise the p110alpha, p110beta, p110gamma, and p110delta catalytic isoforms encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3CG, and PIK3CD, respectively.
Class II PI3Ks differ from class I and III enzymes in lipid products and downstream effectors; the review identifies sortins, small GTPases, and myotubularins as major downstream effectors.
The review characterizes class III PI3K VPS34 as a regulator of autophagy and macrophage phagocytosis through distinct multiprotein complexes.
Akt1, Akt2, and Akt3 are described as having distinct tissue distributions and cancer functions, including roles for Akt2 in migration and invasion and Akt3 in hormone independence.
Table 1 maps class I, II, and III PI3K isoforms to representative downstream effector families and proteins.
Major upstream PI3K/Akt activators described in the review include receptor tyrosine kinases, Toll-like receptors, B-cell antigen receptors, and G-protein-coupled receptors.
Figure 1 depicts ligand- and receptor-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt, PTEN-mediated antagonism of PIP3 signaling, and regulatory inputs from mTORC2, TBK1, TRAF6, ATM, and ATR.
The review argues that resistance to a single receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor can occur because multiple receptor tyrosine kinases may activate PI3K signaling in the same cancer.
PTEN is described as a negative regulator of PI3K signaling that converts PIP3 back to PIP2; PTEN loss or inactivation can permit Akt activation without an exogenous oncogenic stimulus.
The review identifies mTOR, GSK3, FOXO transcription factors, TSC2, and MDM2 among major downstream effectors through which Akt regulates growth, metabolism, survival, and tumor biology.
Figure 2 summarizes Akt-dependent downstream regulation of tumor growth, survival, proliferation, immunity, metabolism, and angiogenesis.
The review describes reciprocal crosstalk between PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling and notes that combined pathway inhibition can suppress tumor growth while feedback interactions complicate targeting.
A regulatory circuit is described between EGFR/PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 and IKK/NF-kappaB signaling, providing a rationale for pathway co-targeting.
The review describes crosstalk between Wnt/beta-catenin and PI3K/Akt signaling, including context-dependent reciprocal effects on pathway activation.
PI3K/Akt signaling is presented as a promoter of tumorigenesis and tumor-cell proliferation through regulation of downstream effectors and cell-cycle control.
The review describes PI3K/Akt signaling as antiapoptotic through phosphorylation-dependent regulation of Bad, procaspase-9, and Bcl-2-family signaling.
Dysregulated PI3K/Akt signaling is described as a contributor to treatment resistance across cancers, including chemotherapy and antiestrogen resistance.
The review links PI3K/Akt activation to PD-L1 regulation and immune-checkpoint resistance and uses this relationship to motivate combinations of checkpoint inhibitors with PI3K-pathway inhibitors.
The PI3K/Akt pathway is described as reprogramming cancer metabolism through nutrient transporters, metabolic enzymes, mTORC1, GSK3, and FOXO transcription factors.
The review describes Akt1 and PI3K p110alpha as regulators of tumor angiogenesis and notes that p110alpha inactivation can impair vascular function and tumor growth in preclinical models.
PI3K/Akt signaling is described as promoting metastasis through reduced intercellular adhesion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, enhanced motility, and tumor neovascularization.
The review notes an important exception to a uniformly prometastatic model: Akt1 can exert antimetastatic effects in some breast-cancer contexts.

Inflammation and PI3K/Akt signaling are described as mutually reinforcing processes that can promote tumor development through inflammatory cells, cytokines, oxidative stress, and endothelial effects.
PI3Kdelta is presented as a central PI3K isoform in adaptive immune signaling through T-cell and B-cell receptors, while Akt activity also influences T-cell metabolic programs and differentiation.

The review describes PI3K/Akt signaling in cancer-associated fibroblasts and endothelial cells as part of the tumor microenvironment and proposes stromal PI3K targeting as a potential complement to conventional therapy.

Figure 3 summarizes the review's proposed links between PI3K/Akt signaling and tumor growth, apoptosis, resistance, metabolism, angiogenesis, metastasis, inflammation, immunity, and the tumor microenvironment.
The authors conclude that PI3K/Akt signaling plays an essential role across multiple cancer phenotypes and therefore provides multiple therapeutic entry points.
The review groups PI3K-directed therapies into pan-PI3K inhibitors, isoform-selective PI3K inhibitors, and dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitors, each with different selectivity and toxicity trade-offs.
The review reports that a phase I study of BKM120 in 35 patients with advanced solid tumors identified a maximum tolerated dose of 100 mg/day and preliminary antitumor activity.

population.label: Patients with advanced solid tumors in the phase I study summarized by the review

exposures.details: Dose-escalation range reported as 12.5-150 mg/day; MTD reported as 100 mg/day.

outcome.definition: Maximum tolerated dose as reported in the phase I study summary.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: A phase I study of 35 patients receiving BKM120 at 12.5-150 mg/day reported an MTD of 100 mg/day.

canonical_statement: The review reports a 29% remission rate with BYL-719 plus fulvestrant among heavily pretreated patients with PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

population.label: Heavily pretreated patients with PIK3CA-mutant tumors summarized by the review

outcome.definition: Remission as summarized by the review.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: The combination of BYL-719 and fulvestrant resulted in remission of 29% of severely pretreated PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

canonical_statement: Table 2 summarizes development phase and reported toxic effects for pan-PI3K, isoform-selective PI3K, and dual PI3K/mTOR inhibitors; recurrent toxicities include hyperglycemia, rash, diarrhea, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and hematologic effects.
The review argues that dual PI3K/mTOR inhibition may reduce feedback reactivation of PI3K signaling but emphasizes uncertainty about tolerability and off-target toxicity.
Table 3 lists pan-Akt and Akt-selective inhibitors in clinical development, including perifosine, GSK-690693, VQD-002, AZD-5363, GDC-0068, GSK-2141795, M2698, GSK-2110183, and MK-2206.
The review describes MK-2206 as an allosteric pan-Akt inhibitor with preclinical synergy alongside several cytotoxic agents and limited early clinical activity in selected tumors.
The review distinguishes rapamycin analogs from ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors and notes that ATP-competitive agents can inhibit both mTORC1 and mTORC2 more completely.
Table 4 organizes selected PI3K/Akt/mTOR inhibitors by cellular process and downstream targets associated with apoptosis, proliferation, and autophagy.

The authors frame combination therapy as a major future direction, especially pairing PI3K/Akt-pathway inhibitors with growth-factor receptor inhibitors, MAPK inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunotherapy.
The review reports that combining PI3K and MAPK pathway inhibitors can improve antitumor efficacy compared with either pathway inhibitor alone, but at the cost of increased toxicity.
PI3K-pathway inhibition is described as a potential chemosensitizing and DNA-repair-modifying strategy, including combinations with cytotoxic chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors.
The review characterizes combinations of PI3K/Akt inhibitors with radiotherapy as promising and cites buparlisib plus radiotherapy in NSCLC as a clinically explored example.
The review describes PI3K/mTOR-inhibitor combinations with immunotherapy as promising but emphasizes that CAR-T enhancement in solid tumors was preliminary and mechanistically unresolved.
The authors identify inhibitor toxicity and adverse effects, including hyperglycemia and rash, as major obstacles to PI3K/Akt-pathway therapy.
The authors question how reliably animal models and in vitro experiments predict clinical toxicity of PI3K/Akt-pathway inhibitors.
The authors state that conventional phase I, II, and III trial models may be poorly suited to evaluation of PI3K inhibitors.
The review concludes that deeper mechanistic understanding of PI3K/Akt signaling is required to manipulate the pathway effectively while managing toxicity and therapeutic resistance.
